Interview
Experience
BNY MELLON

Nisarga Kale
B.Tech Computer Engineering
Procedure
1. Online Assessment(OA)
2. Offline PPT
3. Offline Technical Round
4. Offline HR Round

Online Assessment
The OA consisted of 4 DSA questions which were to be completed within 2 hours.
The questions were as follows:
1. An escape game requires that players solve various puzzles to obtain objects that
will aid them in escaping. In one such puzzle. Players are given an array of integers
and a set of rules to follow in order. Here are the instructions given to the players:
"Given an array of integer values, maximize the points earned using the following
method.
1. Choose a value v. Delete all elements of that value and add their sum to
the points.
2. Delete all elements equal to v-1 or v-2 for no points
3. Repeat steps 1 and 2 until there are no more elements in the array.
Calculate the maximum number of points that can be achieved by following these
rules for an array of values. For example, array = [5, 6, 6, 4, 11], delete 11 for 11
points. Since there are no elements equal to 10 or 12, proceed with the remaining
elements [5, 6, 6, 4]. Delete the two 6s for 12 more points. Delete any elements
equal to 6-1=5 or 6+1=7. Then proceed with the remaining elements: [4]. Finally
delete the 4 and add 4 points for total points 11+12+4=27.
I solved it by using 2D memoized DP with the states being the current index and
previous index, and by using the frequency of each element I calculated the
maximum points possible by taking the current element into score only when
element-1 is not taken, which can be achieved by sorting the array beforehand. I
was able to pass all the testcases.
2. A subarray is a contiguous portion of an array, Given an array of Integers,
determine the number of distinct subarrays that can be formed having at most a
given number of odd elements. Two subarrays are distinct if they differ at even one
position in their contents. Example: Array = [1, 2, 3, 4] The following is a list of the
8 distinct valid subarrays having no more than 1 odd element: [[1], [2], [3], [4], [1,2],
[2, 3], [3, 4], [2, 3, 4]]. Since the constraints of the problem were n<=1000, it was
easily possible to brute force all possible subarrays in O(n^2) and count the odd
elements in that particular subarray. For tougher constraints, a sliding window
approach would be the key to go. I was able to pass all the testcases.
1

3. A subsequence is a sequence that can be derived from another string by deleting
some or no elements, but without changing the order of the remaining
characters.For this puzzle, you need to determine if the second string can be
formed from the first string by removing certain characters, and if so, calculate the
difference value, which represents the index where the transformation of the
second string from the first string occurs. The difference value is the sum of the
index differences between the characters of the second string and the matching
characters from the first string, where the difference is computed as the maximum
index among removed characters in firstString minus the minimum index among
the removed characters in secondString.
Example:
Input:firstString = "HACKERRANK"
secondString = "HACKERMAN"
Output:1
Explanation:
●
To form the secondString = "HACKERMAN" as a subsequence from firstString =
"HACKERRANK", you can remove the character 'M' at index 7 in secondString, and
the remaining string will still be a valid subsequence of firstString which will be
HACKERRAN.
●
The difference value is 7−7+1=0+1=1.
●
Therefore, the function should return 1, indicating the necessary index
transformation.
This problem was on the tougher side, but still I maintained my calm and started
thinking of some approach. I calculated the frequencies of characters in both the
strings and ran a loop over the frequency map of the second string. If the frequency
of the character in the second string was greater than the first string, I added the
difference to the answer else I added the frequency in the second string. I was able
to pass 9 test cases out of 15.
4.
Given a list of employees where each is assigned a numeric evaluation score, use
the selection process below to find the sum of scores of selected employees
2

1. The employee with the highest score among the first k employees or last &
employees in the score list are selected.
2. The selected employee is removed from the score list.
3. The process continues to select the next employee until the team size is
achieved.
Note:
1. In case multiple employees have the same highest score, the employee with the
lowest Index is selected.
2. If there are fewer than k employees, the entire list is available for selection.
Example score [10, 20, 10, 15, 5, 30, 20]
teamSize= 2 k= 3
• For the first selection, choose from the first 3 elements [10, 20, 10] or the last 3
elements: [5, 30, 20] . Score 30 is selected and removed from the list. This makes the score
= [10, 20, 10, 15, 5, 20] For the second selection, choose from [10, 20, 10] or [15, 5, 20] .
Score 20 is selected from the lowest index and removed from the list. This makes score =
[10, 10, 15, 5, 20] The sum of the selected employees' scores is 30+20=50.
I solved this problem with the help of a max priority_queue of {number,flag}, flag was 1 for
first k elements and 0 for last k elements, thus maximum number came to the top and if
equal elements were present, the one with flag 1(among the first k elements) became the
one we choose. I ran a loop for team size removing the numbers from the priority queue
and adding more using two pointers, one for first k elements with flag set and another for
last k elements with flag 0. I was able to pass all the testcases.
I was able to pass all the test cases for three questions and 9 test cases for the third one.
The time allotted was enough and the difficulty of problems was medium-hard.
Offline Pre-Placement Talk
After the Online Assessment (OA), a Pre-Placement Talk (PPT) is usually held for all
applicants. It's important to attend the PPT because it provides crucial information about
3

the company, such as its work culture, values, and locations. This information is often
asked during the HR interview to see if you were attentive. The PPT also helps you come
up with thoughtful questions for the interviewers, which is essential when they ask, "Do
you have any questions for us?" You should always have at least two good questions ready
for this.
The shortlisted students were announced after the PPT.
The first round was purely technical and the second round was taken by a senior person.
Round 1:Technical Interview
I entered the interview room with a smile, a hint of nervousness, and greeted the
interviewer with, "Hello, good morning." He greeted me back, introduced himself, and
began the interview by asking, “Tell me about yourself.”
This is a key question, and it’s important to have a 2-3 minute introduction prepared as it
forms your first impression. I made sure to mention the skills I’m confident in because
interviewers often ask follow-up questions based on your introduction (though not
always).
Next, he asked which data structures I had worked with. I responded with arrays, stacks,
queues, linked lists, trees, and graphs. He followed up by asking which sorting algorithms I
was familiar with. I listed insertion sort, bubble sort, selection sort, merge sort, and quick
sort. He then handed me a pen and paper, asking me to write the code for merge sort and
quicksort. After writing the functions, he gave me a test case and asked me to dry run it
using both methods.
Since he was a Java programmer and not very familiar with C++, he asked me about
vectors, as I had used them in my code. I explained the push and pop operations, and he
asked me to draw the recursion stack for the test case, explaining each step. I walked him
through the recursion calls and showed him the stack correctly.
4

One tip: always explain your thought process aloud so the interviewer can follow your
approach. He then asked me to derive the time complexities for both programs, which I
did.
Moving on, he asked how I practice DSA. I shared that I regularly solve problems on
GeeksforGeeks and LeetCode and participate in contests. When he asked how many
questions I had solved on LeetCode, he was impressed by the number.
The next question was about OOP (Object-Oriented Programming). He asked me to
explain everything I knew about it. Since I had prepared well, I spoke for about five
minutes, covering the four pillars (with real-life examples), classes, objects, access
specifiers, and more. He seemed satisfied with my answer and proceeded to the next
question.
He asked me about the ACID properties in DBMS, and I explained them with real-life
examples. Again, he seemed content with my explanation.
Next, we discussed my projects. He asked if I had worked on them individually or in a team.
One of my projects was done during a hackathon, so he asked about that experience. I
explained that we couldn’t fully complete the project during the hackathon due to time
constraints but finished it afterward. It’s crucial to be honest about your contributions, as
questions will be based on the technologies you mention in your resume.
Since my projects were mostly in web development, he asked questions about JavaScript
and React, including how components are passed in websites and how routing works. I
answered these questions well, and he seemed satisfied.
Before wrapping up, he reviewed my academic scores—my CPI (9.25) and board
percentages—and was impressed. He also asked about my CET score.
Finally, he asked if I had any questions for him. I asked two thoughtful questions, and the
interview ended on a positive note.
5

Round 2:HR Round
The HR round was supposed to focus on situational questions, but for me, it turned out to
be mostly technical. The interviewer first glanced at my projects and asked several
questions based on them.
He asked me to explain what components are and then requested that I list 10 unique
components I’ve observed on various websites. He was very specific about needing 10,
but I could only come up with 6. I was feeling stressed and couldn’t think of more at the
time. He started cross-questioning me on the components I listed and pointed out that
they weren’t unique.
Despite feeling nervous, I made sure not to show it in my body language. I calmly
responded, "Right now, I can’t think of more, but if I remember any, I will let you know." He
seemed to be testing how I handled pressure and cross-questioning.
Next, he asked what I knew about BNY. I recounted what I had learned from the PPT,
which is why it’s so important to attend those talks. He was impressed when I started with
the statement, "It is a bank of banks."
He then asked me about the hackathons and ideathons I had participated in, as I had
mentioned them earlier. Finally, he asked about my family background.
Throughout the interview, he cross-questioned many of my answers, so I wasn’t sure if he
was satisfied with my responses. However, I stayed composed and answered as honestly
as I could.
Result
The result of shortlisted students was announced on the same day.

Preparation
1. Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA): Solve most questions from Striver’s A2Z
sheet, which covers important standard problems across all topics.
2. Database Management Systems (DBMS) & Operating Systems (OS): Focus on
understanding the key concepts in the syllabus. The content from semester 4
should be sufficient for these subjects.
3. Object-Oriented Programming (OOP): Refer to articles on GeeksforGeeks and
practice writing code for each OOP concept.
4. Projects: Be well-versed in your projects and use the STAR (Situation, Task, Action,
Result) method to explain your role and contributions, especially for team projects.
5. Resume: Know your resume thoroughly and anticipate questions related to your
project tech stack (e.g., Firebase, MongoDB, React) using resources like
InterviewBit or GeeksforGeeks.
6. CS Fundamentals: Revise core concepts in Operating Systems, OOP, and DBMS. If
time permits, also review Computer Networks (CN) and low/high-level design
concepts.
7. Additional Resources: Seek help from seniors for resume reviews and mock
interviews.
8. Dressing for Interviews: Dress appropriately for in-person interviews, as a
professional appearance is crucial.
